extracted.intended_audience: general readers and students of elementary astronomy (readers with some familiarity with basic geometry/trigonometry)
extracted.subtask_description: A textbook chapter explaining the physical conditions that produce solar and lunar eclipses and the practical requirements for predicting their times, types, durations, and local appearances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: eclipse of the moon
rubrics_metrics.description: An eclipse of the moon happens when the moon, in its revolution around the earth, falls into the earth's shadow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Occurs at full moon (opposition). The moon first enters the penumbra (partial dimming) then the umbra (full shadow). Even in total lunar eclipses the moon remains visible with a dull red light due to refraction of sunlight through Earth's atmosphere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: eclipse of the sun
rubrics_metrics.description: An eclipse of the sun happens when the moon, coming between the earth and the sun, covers either a part or the whole of the solar disk.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Occurs only at new moon (conjunction). Observer-dependent: the sun may be totally hidden for some observers and only partially obscured or fully visible for others a few miles away.

rubrics_metrics.name: Phase condition for eclipses (new/full)
rubrics_metrics.description: An eclipse of the sun can take place only at new moon; an eclipse of the moon can occur only at full moon (when sun and moon are in conjunction or opposition respectively).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Phase alone is not sufficient — the relative position with respect to the moon's orbital nodes must also place the bodies near the ecliptic plane for an eclipse to occur.

rubrics_metrics.name: Orbital inclination and node proximity requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The moon's orbit is inclined about five degrees to the ecliptic, so eclipses occur only when the new or full moon is sufficiently near one of the moon's nodes (the two points where its orbit cuts the ecliptic).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the combined semidiameters of sun and moon (and/or Earth's shadow and moon) reach only about half to three quarters of the five-degree separation, conjunction/opposition must be near a node. The nodes retrograde (~19.5° per year), and their motion determines recurrence patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shadow geometry: umbra and penumbra and cone lengths
rubrics_metrics.description: Both the earth and moon cast conical shadows (umbra and penumbra) because the sun has finite size; the moon's shadow at average distance just reaches the earth; the earth's shadow is nearly a million miles long and about three times as broad as the moon at lunar distance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Penumbra produces partial eclipses; umbra produces total eclipses. The geometry (cone length, where the moon intersects the shadow) controls whether an eclipse is total, partial, or annular and how it appears to observers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of moon's distance on eclipse type (total vs annular) and shadow size
rubrics_metrics.description: The moon's apparent diameter varies with distance: when nearer (perigee) its shadow can reach beyond the Earth's surface producing total eclipses; when further (apogee) its shadow may be too short and an annular eclipse (a ring of sun around moon) results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When moon is at perigee and Earth near aphelion the lunar shadow can extend ~15,000 miles beyond Earth's center and cover ~170 miles on the surface. Maximum durations: total solar eclipses seldom exceed eight minutes; annular eclipses at most 12 minutes 24 seconds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local circumstances and path-of-totality requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Because the moon's umbral shadow covers only a narrow path on Earth's surface (commonly much less than 170 miles) and moves rapidly (~2,280 miles per hour), the precise character of a solar eclipse (total, annular, partial) must be calculated for each place separately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Earth's rotation and relative motion of the shadow determine the local timing, quantity, and duration of the eclipse; small changes in observer location can change whether an eclipse is total, annular, or partial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for accurate lunar and solar position tables
rubrics_metrics.description: To predict eclipses astronomers determine the exact positions the sun and moon will occupy in the heavens at future times using long-continued observations summarized in tables of their motions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One first finds the mean place (uniform circular motion), then applies corrections (equations) for irregularities to obtain the true place. Tables give node positions and all necessary elements to decide proximity to nodes and relative longitudes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical prerequisites for eclipse calculation
rubrics_metrics.description: The method of calculating eclipses cannot be fully understood without knowledge of trigonometry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beyond trigonometry, the calculation requires combining observational data with geometry and celestial mechanics; for solar eclipses, computing local elements (contacts, magnitude, duration) is more complex and tedious than for lunar eclipses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of the Saros cycle for eclipse recurrence prediction
rubrics_metrics.description: The Saros is a period of about 18 years and 10 days (≈6585.78 days) after which the sun, moon, and lunar node return to nearly the same relative geometry, so eclipses repeat in a similar manner every Saros.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Numerically: 346.619851 days × 19 ≈ 6585.78 days ≈ 223 × 29.5305887 (synodic month). Eclipses separated by a Saros occur in corresponding years and similar order, though magnitudes and exact circumstances differ.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of the Metonic cycle for lunar age and calendar purposes
rubrics_metrics.description: The Metonic cycle consists of 19 tropical years during which there are exactly 235 new moons, so new/full moons recur at the same seasons of the year after 19 years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used historically for fixing the 'age' of the moon for calendars and festivals; yields the 'golden number' denoting the year within the lunar cycle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frequency limits and visibility differences
rubrics_metrics.description: In any year the number of eclipses of both luminaries cannot be less than two nor more than seven; the most usual number is four.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Solar eclipses are globally more frequent than lunar eclipses, but because solar eclipses are visible only along a narrow track they are less often seen from a given place; lunar eclipses are visible from the entire hemisphere opposite the sun so are more commonly observed from a single location.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need to account for lunar irregularities and secular/periodical inequalities
rubrics_metrics.description: The moon's motion exhibits many irregularities (periodical and secular); astronomical tables list values for dozens of these inequalities and apply corrections when finding the moon's true place.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some irregularities are minute and often only ~28–30 terms are used in practice though ~60 exist; secular changes (e.g., small acceleration in moon's mean motion) must be accounted for — La Place showed some long-term accelerations arise from solar disturbing forces linked to Earth's orbital eccentricity.
